title: NoSQL & Modern Databases
summary: The web outgrew rows and columns. Learn why NoSQL emerged, how each of the four families works, when NewSQL changes the equation, and how to model data without joins.

blocks.markdown:
**NoSQL** ("not only SQL") is a broad label for non-relational databases that trade some relational guarantees for scale, flexibility, or speed.

- Born in the 2000s to handle web-scale data that relational stores struggled with.
- Four main families: **key-value**, **document**, **wide-column**, **graph**.
- **NewSQL** brings horizontal scale back with full ACID.
- [data-models](data-models) covers the intro; this topic goes deeper.

Three forces drove the shift away from relational-only architectures in the 2000s.

- **Web-scale writes** — millions of concurrent users writing simultaneously overwhelmed single-server relational engines.
- **Schema rigidity** — social/user-generated content has unpredictable shapes; ALTER TABLE on a billion-row table is dangerous.
- **Horizontal scale** — SQL joins assume all data lives on one machine; NoSQL was designed to shard across hundreds.

Google (Bigtable, 2006) and Amazon (Dynamo, 2007) published the papers that launched the movement.

blocks.subTitle: The four families at a glance
blocks.markdown:
Each family fits a distinct data shape.

| Family | Data shape | Real system |
|---|---|---|
| Key-value | Opaque bytes behind a key | Redis, DynamoDB |
| Document | JSON/BSON tree per record | MongoDB, Firestore |
| Wide-column | Sparse rows with many columns | Cassandra, HBase |
| Graph | Nodes + typed edges | Neo4j, Amazon Neptune |

A **key-value store** is a giant distributed hash map: store any bytes under a key, retrieve them in O(1).

- The engine knows nothing about the value's structure — it's an opaque blob.
- Strength: **extreme read/write throughput** and trivial horizontal partitioning (route key to shard by hash).
- When to use: **session tokens**, **feature flags**, **rate-limit counters**, **caches** in front of slower stores.
- **Redis** adds types (lists, sorted sets, streams) so it's richer than a pure KV, but the core model is the same.

A **document store** groups related data into a single self-describing **document** (usually JSON or BSON).

- Fields can vary per document — a product doc can have `color` that an event doc lacks.
- Supports **rich queries** inside the document (find all users where `address.city = 'Mumbai'`).
- Strength: **locality** — one read fetches a whole entity without joins.
- When to use: **catalogs**, **user profiles**, **CMS content**, **event logs**.
- **MongoDB** is the canonical example; **Firestore** suits mobile apps with its real-time subscriptions.

A **wide-column store** looks like a table but each row can have a different set of columns — columns are stored together on disk per row, not across rows.

- Designed for **petabyte-scale** append-heavy workloads: sensor telemetry, audit logs, time-series.
- Reads are fast when you access a whole row (all columns) but slow for scanning a single column across many rows.
- **Cassandra** (peer-to-peer, no single master) handles millions of writes/sec; **HBase** (HDFS-backed) suits Hadoop ecosystems.
- Key design insight: **partition key** determines which node holds the row — design it around your most common read.

A **graph database** stores **nodes** (entities) and **edges** (typed, directed relationships between them), both with properties.

- Traversing edges is O(1) per hop — no join tables, no index scans.
- SQL equivalent of a 6-hop friend-of-friend query is 6 joins that compound; graph walks it directly.
- When to use: **fraud detection** (rings of shared accounts), **recommendation engines**, **dependency graphs**, **access-control hierarchies**.
- **Neo4j** uses Cypher query language; **Amazon Neptune** supports both Gremlin and SPARQL.
- Weakness: poor for bulk analytics across all nodes (graph is optimized for traversal, not aggregation).

**NewSQL** systems provide the horizontal scale of NoSQL while preserving full **ACID** transactions and SQL query support.

- **ACID** (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) means transactions are correct even when nodes fail mid-write.
- Classic relational engines scale vertically (bigger machine); NewSQL scales horizontally across data centers.
- **Google Spanner** — global distributed SQL, uses TrueTime for linearizable commits. **CockroachDB** — open-source Spanner-like, Postgres-compatible wire protocol.
- When to use: financial systems or multi-region apps that need joins + correctness + geographic distribution.
- Trade-off: higher latency than eventually-consistent NoSQL due to coordination overhead. See [cap-consistency-base](cap-consistency-base).

Choosing between SQL and NoSQL comes down to four axes.

| Axis | Prefer SQL | Prefer NoSQL |
|---|---|---|
| Consistency | Strong ACID required | Eventual OK |
| Query pattern | Ad-hoc joins, aggregations | Predictable key lookups |
| Schema | Stable, well-known | Evolving, user-defined |
| Scale | Vertical, moderate size | Horizontal, massive writes |

Neither wins universally — match the tool to the workload.

blocks.subTitle: Denormalization
blocks.markdown:
Relational modeling **normalizes** — splits data to eliminate redundancy. NoSQL often **denormalizes** — duplicates data to eliminate joins.

- A social-post document might embed the author's name directly, even though the user collection also has it.
- The trade-off: writes update more places, but reads are a single fetch with no join.
- Rule of thumb: **read-heavy** paths justify denormalization; **write-heavy** paths make it costly.

See [sharding-replication-scaling](sharding-replication-scaling) for how denormalized data is distributed.

blocks.subTitle: Model around your queries
blocks.markdown:
In NoSQL, the question "how will I read this?" drives schema design — the opposite of relational.

- Cassandra: the **partition key + clustering columns** must match your query's WHERE clause. You design the table for one access pattern.
- DynamoDB: single table design groups multiple entity types under one table, accessed by composite keys.
- A pattern change often means creating a new table (or index), not rewriting a query.

This is why NoSQL schemas feel "locked in" despite being schema-less at the engine level.

**Polyglot persistence** means using multiple database types in one system, each handling what it does best.

- **Polyglot**: Greek for "many languages" — here, many data stores.
- Example: an e-commerce app might use Postgres for orders (ACID), Redis for cart sessions (fast KV), Elasticsearch for product search (inverted index), and Neo4j for recommendations (graph).
- Each service or bounded context owns its store — a microservices pattern.
- Cost: **operational complexity** (more systems to monitor, backup, and tune) and **cross-store consistency** (no single transaction spans them).

Common expert-level mistakes with NoSQL.

- **Modeling NoSQL like a relational DB.** Designing normalized tables, then adding joins in code — worst of both worlds.
- **Ignoring the CAP trade-off.** Eventual consistency causes real bugs: stale reads, double-charges. See [cap-consistency-base](cap-consistency-base).
- **Wrong family for the problem.** Using a document store for deeply connected data means painful multi-query hops instead of one graph traversal.
- **Underestimating fan-out writes.** Denormalized copies must stay in sync — a user rename can touch thousands of documents.

blocks.subTitle: SQL vs NoSQL
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: When would you pick NoSQL over SQL?**

When any of these dominate: (1) horizontal write scale beyond one machine, (2) schema evolves rapidly per record, (3) the access pattern is a single-key lookup with no joins needed, (4) eventual consistency is acceptable. Relational remains default for financial data, reporting, or complex ad-hoc queries.

blocks.subTitle: The four families
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Name the four NoSQL families and a use case for each.**

- **Key-value** (Redis) — session storage, rate limiting.
- **Document** (MongoDB) — user profiles, product catalogs.
- **Wide-column** (Cassandra) — time-series telemetry, activity feeds.
- **Graph** (Neo4j) — fraud detection, social recommendations.

blocks.subTitle: NewSQL
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is NewSQL and when does it win?**

**NewSQL** (e.g., Spanner, CockroachDB) gives you horizontal scale AND full ACID SQL — something classic relational can't do. It wins when you need multi-region consistency + SQL expressiveness: financial ledgers, global inventory, or any system where eventual consistency causes correctness bugs but you've outgrown a single Postgres node.

blocks.subTitle: Polyglot persistence
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is polyglot persistence and what does it cost?**

**Polyglot persistence** is using multiple database types in one system — each for its strength (Postgres for orders, Redis for cache, Elasticsearch for search). The cost is **operational complexity**: more systems to run, monitor, and back up, plus **no cross-store transactions**, so consistency across stores must be handled at the application layer.
